analysis.one_liner: Creates a government office to manufacture affordable generic drugs like insulin and naloxone.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and no other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created an Office of Drug Manufacturing inside the Department of Health and Human Services. That office would manufacture prescription drugs — starting with insulin, naloxone, and antibiotics — and sell them at a price the office judged fair, targeting drugs that are scarce, expensive, or made by fewer than three companies. It would also manufacture key drug ingredients to help generic drug makers enter the market, and it would bar former drug-company lobbyists and executives of companies under federal enforcement from working in the office.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who cannot afford prescription drugs, especially people who need insulin or overdose-reversing naloxone; Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal and state health programs that pay drug prices; and taxpayers who fund those programs. Generic drug companies would also benefit from a new public supplier of hard-to-get active ingredients.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Office of Drug Manufacturing within HHS whose stated purpose is to increase competition, lower prices, and address shortages of prescription drugs, including insulin, naloxone, and antibiotics [S2][S3].
Requires the government to begin publicly manufacturing insulin within a year of enactment, along with naloxone for community use and at least three antibiotics [S3].

Targets drugs in particularly bad markets: off-patent drugs made by fewer than three companies that have seen price increases above inflation, appear on the drug shortage list, or are essential medicines priced out of patients' reach [S3].
Directs the office to manufacture active pharmaceutical ingredients that are not readily available, which would make it easier for other companies to enter the generic drug market [S3].
Bars former drug-company lobbyists and former senior executives of drug manufacturers under federal enforcement action from running or working in the office for six years [S3].

If a buyer of a publicly developed drug application raises the price above the fair price plus inflation, or fails to market the drug, the government can revoke the application and resume production itself [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and generic drug manufacturers would face a new public competitor selling drugs at prices set with patient access and program costs in mind. Taxpayers would fund the office's start-up costs, since the bill authorizes whatever appropriations are needed, though sales revenue would go back into the office's activities.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes unlimited appropriations to build and run a government drug manufacturing operation, so taxpayers would carry the start-up costs before any sales revenue came back in [S3].

Government manufacturing of drugs is untested at this scale: the office would have to win FDA approvals, acquire manufacturing rights, and hit quotas of 15 drugs within one year and 25 within three, an aggressive timeline critics could reasonably call unrealistic [S3].
For antibiotics, the bill itself acknowledges a public-health tradeoff — it requires an annual CDC and FDA assessment of how expanded antibiotic manufacturing affects antimicrobial resistance [S3].

Public manufacturing applies only to drugs with expired patents and exclusivities or drugs the government can license, so it would not touch prices on patented brand-name drugs, the largest driver of new drug costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: a public manufacturer would give the government a direct tool against high prices, shortages, and abandoned off-patent drugs like insulin, rather than relying on negotiation with manufacturers. The main costs are the upfront taxpayer investment, the difficulty of standing up drug manufacturing quickly, and the limits of the approach — it cannot lower prices on drugs still under patent. The bill gives no estimate of what the office would cost, which makes the tradeoff hard to judge from the text alone.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee the week it was introduced, and it sat there with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on December 19, 2019, near the end of the first session of the 116th Congress [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which referred it to the Subcommittee on Health the next day [S5].
No further action was taken for the rest of the Congress: the bill never received a hearing, a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S5].
No other representative cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off, because no public competitor was created and no new pressure was placed on drug prices. The bill died without ever being considered, so nothing about the drug market changed.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled it for a hearing or a committee vote; it remained in the Health Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and no member besides the sponsor supported the bill publicly, so the partisan shape of the opposition never showed up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have created a government-run manufacturer selling drugs at prices set for patient access and program savings, directly competing with manufacturers on shortage-prone and price-gouged drugs. It also would have let the government acquire rights to manufacture drugs, threatening makers who charge prices the Secretary deems a barrier to access [S3].

industries.industry: Generic drug makers and would-be market entrants
industries.note: The office would manufacture scarce active pharmaceutical ingredients and sell them to other entities, lowering a key barrier that keeps new companies out of the generic market [S3].
Former registered drug manufacturer lobbyists would be barred from working in the new office for six years, cutting off one revolving-door path into a powerful new agency [S3].
